summary: At 6,752 feet in the San Bernardino Mountains, Big Bear Lake sits high enough that its annual average high of just 58°F makes it one of the coolest incorporated places in Southern California — a genuine four-season mountain town where winter brings reliable snow and summer afternoons rarely crack 85°F, all under a generous 10.2 hours of daily sunshine that keeps the alpine setting from feeling gloomy. The lake itself, a roughly three-mile-long reservoir ringed by ponderosa pine and granite, functions as the town's gravitational center; Bear Mountain and Snow Summit ski areas anchor the winter economy, while the water draws boaters and anglers the rest of the year. That tourism dependency is the defining tradeoff: the service and hospitality sector dominates employment, and with a median household income of about $74,700 against a median home value near $518,000 — a ratio above 6.9-to-1 — purchasing a home on local wages alone is a stretch, though median rent around $1,278 remains notably lower than most of metro Southern California. The town's roughly 5,000 year-round residents share 6.4 square miles along the south shore, giving the place a quiet, spread-out feel where the commercial strip along Big Bear Boulevard is the only real corridor and evening activity is sparse outside peak tourist weekends. Big Bear Lake is essentially a resort economy that happens to have a permanent population, and living here full-time means embracing both the serenity and the seasonal whiplash that arrangement creates.
